435:
Hebrew was written with consonants only. The Masoretes ('keepers of the tradition') recorded the traditional pronunciation with dots and dashes, and added accents for chanting and phrasing. Their margin notes (the *Masorah*) count letters, words and unusual spellings, note the middle verse of books, and flag places where the text written (*ketiv*) should be read differently (*qere*).

The ben Asher family of Tiberias became the most respected school. Their system produced the Masoretic Text, the basis of nearly all modern Hebrew Bibles. The Dead Sea Scrolls showed that the consonantal text the Masoretes preserved goes back, in its main form, to well before the time of Jesus.
438: Monks in northern England produced a giant single-volume Latin Bible, the oldest complete Vulgate, as a gift for the pope.
439: Abbot Ceolfrith had three great Bibles made; one was carried toward Rome in 716, but Ceolfrith died on the way. The book later reached the monastery of Monte Amiata in Italy, hence its name, and is now in Florence. For a long time it was thought to be Italian, until a 19th-century scholar showed its dedication had been altered. It weighs about 34 kg and shows the high standard of Anglo-Saxon book-making in the age of Bede.
440: Cyril and Methodius bring the Bible to the Slavs
442: Two brothers from Thessalonica created the Glagolitic alphabet and translated the Gospels and liturgy into Old Church Slavonic.
443: Sent by the Byzantine emperor at the request of the Moravian prince Rastislav, Constantine (later called Cyril) and Methodius insisted on worship in the people's language, defending this against critics who allowed only Hebrew, Greek and Latin. Their disciples later developed the Cyrillic alphabet, named in Cyril's honour. Their work underlies the Bible and liturgy of Russian, Serbian, Bulgarian and other Slavic churches.
446: The finest Masoretic Bible, pointed by Aaron ben Asher around 930; Maimonides praised it as the model copy.
447: The codex was kept for centuries in Jerusalem, Cairo and then Aleppo. In 1947 riots in Aleppo damaged the synagogue, and when the codex reached Israel (by 1958) about 40 percent was missing, including most of the Torah. How the missing pages disappeared is still unclear. It is the basis of the Hebrew University Bible Project edition.
450: The oldest complete Hebrew Bible, copied in 1008, is the base text of the standard scholarly Hebrew Bible editions used for most modern translations.
451: Copied by Samuel ben Jacob, it follows the ben Asher tradition. It is called Leningrad because it is held in the National Library of Russia in St Petersburg (formerly Leningrad). It is the base of *Biblia Hebraica Stuttgartensia* and *Biblia Hebraica Quinta*.
454: The chapter numbers used in Bibles today go back mainly to Stephen Langton, who devised them while teaching in Paris before becoming Archbishop of Canterbury in 1207.
455:
Earlier manuscripts had various section systems, but none was universal. Langton's chapters spread through the 'Paris Bibles' produced for students in the 13th century and became standard. Dates for the system are given anywhere from about 1203 to 1227 (the year Langton's system is sometimes associated with), because it was worked out and spread over time.

Chapters are useful but not inspired: some break in odd places, for example splitting Isaiah 52:13-53:12 or separating 1 Corinthians 13 from its context.
456: The Wycliffe Bible: first complete English Bible
458: Followers of John Wycliffe produced the first complete Bible in English, translated from the Latin Vulgate and copied by hand.
459: An early, very literal version (around 1382) was followed by a smoother later version (around 1388-1395), often linked with John Purvey. Wycliffe argued that ordinary Christians should read scripture for themselves. In 1407-1409 Archbishop Arundel's Constitutions forbade making or reading new English translations without approval, and Wycliffe's remains were later dug up and burned (1428). Even so, around 250 manuscripts survive, showing wide use.
462: Johannes Gutenberg's movable-type press produced a Latin Vulgate Bible around 1454-1455, the first major book printed in Europe.
463: About 180 copies were printed, some on paper and some on vellum; around 49 survive in whole or in part. Printing meant that identical copies could be produced quickly and far more cheaply than by hand, which made later vernacular Bibles and Reformation debates possible on a large scale. It also froze texts: errors could be multiplied as easily as truth.
464: Erasmus publishes the Greek New Testament
466: Erasmus' Greek New Testament with a new Latin translation was the first published Greek New Testament. Its later editions became the basis of the 'Textus Receptus' behind the KJV.
467:
Rushed into print by the publisher Froben, the first edition used a handful of late medieval manuscripts available in Basel. For the last six verses of Revelation, missing in his manuscript, Erasmus translated the Latin back into Greek. (The Complutensian Polyglot was printed earlier, in 1514, but published only around 1520-1522.)

Erasmus revised the text through five editions. In his third edition (1522) he added the Comma Johanneum (1 John 5:7-8) after a Greek manuscript containing it was produced. Printed Greek texts by Estienne, Beza and the Elzevirs followed Erasmus closely; the Elzevir edition of 1633 called itself the text 'now received by all', giving us the name *Textus Receptus*.
470: Hiding in the Wartburg, Martin Luther translated the New Testament from Erasmus' Greek in about eleven weeks (published September 1522); the full Bible followed in 1534.
471: Luther aimed for German that ordinary people spoke, 'looking at the mouth' of the mother at home and the man in the market. His Bible shaped the modern German language. He placed Hebrews, James, Jude and Revelation at the end of his New Testament, and in early prefaces called James 'an epistle of straw' compared with the books that most clearly show Christ, though he kept them in his Bible. He gathered the books outside the Hebrew canon into a separate section called Apocrypha, 'not held equal to Holy Scripture, but useful and good to read'.
474: William Tyndale translated the New Testament from Greek, the first English New Testament printed and the first translated from the original language. Copies were smuggled into England and burned by authorities.
475:
Tyndale reportedly told a cleric he would cause a boy who drives the plough to know more scripture than he did. A first printing at Cologne in 1525 was interrupted; the complete octavo edition came out at Worms in 1526. He went on to translate the Pentateuch (1530), Jonah and other Old Testament books from Hebrew.

His choices, such as 'congregation' for *ekklesia* instead of 'church', 'elder' instead of 'priest', and 'repent' instead of 'do penance', were attacked by Thomas More as heretical. Tyndale coined or popularised phrases like 'let there be light', 'the powers that be' and 'scapegoat'. Studies estimate that most of the KJV New Testament wording follows Tyndale.
476: Coverdale: first complete printed English Bible
478: Miles Coverdale published the first complete printed Bible in English, using Tyndale's work where it existed and German and Latin versions for the rest.
479: Coverdale did not know Hebrew or Greek well and said so openly. His Psalms, with their musical rhythm, were later used in the Great Bible (1539), the first English Bible authorised for reading in churches, and were kept in the Book of Common Prayer for centuries. His Bible placed the deuterocanonical books in a separate section, a pattern followed in later Protestant Bibles.
482: Betrayed by Henry Phillips, Tyndale was imprisoned, condemned for heresy, strangled and burned. His reported last prayer was that God would open the King of England's eyes.
483: Within a few years, English Bibles largely built on his work (Matthew's Bible 1537, the Great Bible 1539) were licensed in England by Henry VIII, so many see his prayer as answered. The prayer is reported by John Foxe; exact wording should be treated as tradition.
484: Council of Trent defines the Catholic canon
486: On 8 April 1546 the Council of Trent declared a list of sacred books including Tobit, Judith, Wisdom, Sirach, Baruch, 1-2 Maccabees and the Greek additions to Esther and Daniel, and declared the Vulgate 'authentic' for public use.
487: Earlier Western councils (Hippo, Carthage, Florence in 1442) had given similar lists, but Trent made the canon a binding definition with anathema, in response to Protestant reformers who followed the Hebrew canon. 'Authentic' for the Vulgate meant reliable for doctrine in public use, not that it was free from every copying error; an official revised Vulgate followed (Sixto-Clementine, 1592). The Prayer of Manasseh and 1-2 Esdras were placed in an appendix.
488: Robert Estienne numbers New Testament verses
490: The printer Robert Estienne (Stephanus) introduced the New Testament verse numbers we still use in his 1551 Greek-Latin New Testament.
491: His son later said he worked them out on a journey from Paris to Lyon, some say on horseback, which has been blamed for odd breaks, though that is anecdote. Old Testament verses already existed as units in the Hebrew Masoretic tradition, and had been numbered in a 15th-century Hebrew concordance by Rabbi Isaac Nathan; Estienne's 1553 French Bible was the first full Bible numbered throughout with chapters and verses. Verse numbers make reference easy but can encourage reading single sentences out of context.
493: English Protestant exiles in Geneva produced a readable, affordable Bible with verse numbers, maps and extensive study notes. It was the Bible of Shakespeare, the Puritans and the Pilgrims.
494: Led by William Whittingham, the translators revised Tyndale and the Great Bible against Greek and Hebrew. It was the first complete English Bible with verse numbers throughout and roman type. Its Calvinist margin notes, some of which questioned obedience to tyrannical kings, made James I dislike it, which partly explains why he backed a new translation without such notes. It remained popular for decades after 1611.
497: English Catholic scholars in exile translated the Vulgate into English: the New Testament at Rheims (1582) and the Old Testament at Douai (1609-1610).
498: Led by Gregory Martin, the translators stayed very close to Latin, coining words like 'supersubstantial bread' and keeping technical terms. Their New Testament influenced some KJV word choices. It was revised by Bishop Richard Challoner in 1749-1752, the form most Catholics later used.
501: Commissioned at the Hampton Court Conference (1604), about 47 scholars in six companies revised the Bishops' Bible against Hebrew and Greek, producing the most influential English translation in history.
502: The translators' preface says they did not aim to make a new translation, nor a bad one good, but a good one better. It drew heavily on Tyndale and Geneva. The New Testament followed the Textus Receptus tradition of Erasmus, Estienne and Beza. The original 1611 edition included the Apocrypha. The text most people read today is the 1769 Oxford revision by Benjamin Blayney, with modernised spelling and many small corrections. Despite the name, it was never formally 'authorised' by an act that survives on record.
505: The Westminster Confession listed the 66 books and said the Apocrypha are not inspired and have no authority beyond other human writings.
506: Earlier, the Church of England's Thirty-Nine Articles (1563/1571) had kept the Apocrypha as books read 'for example of life and instruction of manners' but not to establish doctrine. Over the 19th century, Bible societies stopped printing the Apocrypha in most Protestant Bibles, which is why many modern Protestants never see these books.
509: John Mill's Greek New Testament gathered readings from about 100 manuscripts and noted some 30,000 differences, alarming some readers and starting modern textual criticism.
510: Richard Bentley replied that more manuscripts mean more variants but also more ability to find the original, and that most differences are trivial. Later scholars such as Bengel (1734) and Griesbach (from 1774) developed rules for weighing readings (for example, the harder reading is often older). Today scholars estimate several hundred thousand variant readings across more than 5,800 Greek manuscripts; the large majority are spelling, word order or obvious slips, and very few affect meaning in ways that are both meaningful and plausibly original.
513: Constantin von Tischendorf took 43 leaves of an ancient Greek Bible from St Catherine's in 1844 and in 1859 was shown much more of it, including the complete New Testament, which he brought to the Russian tsar.
514: Tischendorf's famous story that the leaves were in a basket about to be burned is disputed; the monks reject it, and parchment does not burn well. The 1859 transfer to Russia was presented as a loan that became a gift; whether it was fairly obtained remains a sore point for the monastery. In 1933 the Soviet government sold most of the codex to the British Museum. In 1975 more leaves were found in a sealed room at the monastery. Since 2009 the whole surviving codex has been online, reunited digitally.
515: Westcott and Hort's Greek text and the Revised Version
517: Two Cambridge scholars published a Greek New Testament based mainly on Vaticanus and Sinaiticus, and the English Revised Version New Testament appeared the same year.
518:
B. F. Westcott and F. J. A. Hort spent 28 years on their edition. They grouped manuscripts into text-types and argued that the 'Syrian' (Byzantine) text, the majority of later manuscripts, was a later smoothed-out form, while the 'Neutral' text of Vaticanus and Sinaiticus was closest to the original. Their method still shapes modern editions, though their idea of a 'Neutral' text has been revised.

Dean John Burgon attacked both the text and the Revised Version fiercely, defending the traditional text; his arguments are still used by defenders of the Majority Text and the Textus Receptus.
520: The Revised Version, the first officially approved revision of the KJV, was completed in 1885 (Old Testament) after its 1881 New Testament.
521: Its New Testament sold millions on publication day, but its stiff, very literal English never displaced the KJV in popular use. It began the long line of modern English revisions.
524: Bernard Grenfell and Arthur Hunt began digging ancient rubbish mounds in Egypt and recovered hundreds of thousands of papyrus fragments, including early New Testament papyri and the *Gospel of Thomas* in Greek.
525: The dry sand preserved documents of daily life alongside literary and Christian texts. Dozens of New Testament papyri (from the 2nd to 7th centuries) have come from Oxyrhynchus, showing that Christians in a provincial town had many books. Publication continues to this day.
526: Eberhard Nestle's handy Greek New Testament
528: Nestle published a pocket Greek New Testament built by comparing the leading critical editions; its descendant, the Nestle-Aland edition, is now the standard text.
529: Kurt Aland joined the project after World War II. The 27th edition (1993) and 28th (2012) of Nestle-Aland share their main text with the United Bible Societies' *Greek New Testament* (first edition 1966, 5th 2014), which was designed for translators. Together they underlie most modern translations.
532: The American edition of the Revised Version, with the American committee's preferences, including 'Jehovah' for God's name.
533: Prized for its precision, it became the base for the RSV, the NASB and (through the Living Bible's paraphrase) the NLT's ancestor.
536: W. L. Nash bought a small papyrus with the Ten Commandments and the Shema in Hebrew, the oldest known Hebrew biblical text until the Dead Sea Scrolls.
537: Dated to roughly the 2nd or 1st century BC, it is probably a liturgical or teaching sheet rather than a biblical scroll. Its order of commandments matches some Septuagint manuscripts, an early hint that the Hebrew text once had more variety.
540: A collection of 3rd-century papyrus codices containing the Gospels and Acts, Paul's letters and Revelation, plus Greek Old Testament books, was made public.
541: These codices (P45, P46, P47 among them) pushed the evidence for large parts of the New Testament back more than a century earlier than the great 4th-century codices. Part of P46 is held by the University of Michigan.
544: C. H. Roberts recognised a scrap bought in Egypt in 1920 as part of John 18, often called the oldest known New Testament fragment.
545: Roberts published it in 1935, dating it to the first half of the 2nd century on handwriting. Later scholars have widened the range to roughly 125-175, and some (such as Brent Nongbri) argue a date as late as around 200 cannot be ruled out. Handwriting dating gives ranges, not exact years.
546: Wycliffe Bible Translators and the global translation movement
548: William Cameron Townsend founded Wycliffe Bible Translators (with the linguistics school SIL) to translate the Bible into languages without one. Translation has accelerated sharply since.
549:
Bible societies (the British and Foreign Bible Society from 1804, the American Bible Society from 1816) had already spread translations widely. Townsend's experience in Guatemala, where a man asked why, if God was so great, he did not speak his language, shaped the mission.

Counts change every year. Wycliffe Global Alliance figures for 2023-2024 put the full Bible in roughly 740-760 languages, the New Testament in about 1,650-1,750 more, and some portions in over 1,200 more, out of more than 7,000 living languages. Hundreds of millions of people still lack a full Bible in their first language. Treat exact numbers as approximate and check current statistics.
551: Qumran caves, near the Dead Sea
552: A Bedouin shepherd found clay jars holding scrolls in a cave near Qumran. Over the next decade eleven caves yielded remains of some 900 or more manuscripts.
553: The first seven scrolls included the Great Isaiah Scroll. Before 1947, the oldest substantial Hebrew Bible manuscripts were from around AD 900-1000; the scrolls pushed the evidence back about a thousand years. They showed both remarkable stability in many books (Isaiah is very close to the medieval text) and real variety in others (Jeremiah exists in a shorter form like the Septuagint's). Full publication was slow and controversial; all were available by the early 2000s.
555: The RSV revised the American Standard Version in modern English, using the new manuscript discoveries. It was widely used and fiercely attacked.
556: The New Testament appeared in 1946. Critics objected especially to 'young woman' instead of 'virgin' in Isaiah 7:14, and some copies were publicly burned. Defenders noted the Hebrew word *almah* means young woman, while Matthew follows the Greek *parthenos*. The RSV later had a Catholic edition (1966) and an Ecumenical edition, and was revised as the NRSV (1989). The ESV (2001) also began from it.
559: Papyri bought by collector Martin Bodmer included P66 (John, published 1956) and P75 (Luke and John, published 1961), among the earliest substantial Gospel manuscripts.
560: P75's text is strikingly close to Codex Vaticanus, written over a century later. That finding persuaded many scholars that the Vaticanus-type text was not a 4th-century revision but a carefully preserved older text, strengthening the approach of Westcott and Hort. P75 was given to the Vatican Library in 2007.
563: A conservative, very literal update of the ASV, popular for close study.
564: The New Testament came out in 1963 and the full Bible in 1971; it was updated in 1995 and 2020. It keeps close to Greek and Hebrew word order and uses italics for words supplied in English.
567: An evangelical, transdenominational team produced the NIV, aiming for a balance between accuracy and natural English. It became the best-selling modern English Bible.
568: The New Testament appeared in 1973. The NIV was revised in 1984 and 2011; the 2011 update's gender language (for example 'brothers and sisters' where the Greek includes both) drew both praise and criticism. Its translation committee (the Committee on Bible Translation) continues to review it.
571: Updated the KJV's language while keeping its Textus Receptus base, with footnotes giving Critical Text and Majority Text readings.
572: It is a choice for readers who prefer the traditional text but want modern pronouns and verb forms. Its notes are a simple way for non-specialists to see where the main Greek text traditions differ.
575: An ecumenical revision of the RSV used widely in academic and mainline settings, with inclusive language for people.
576: It used the Dead Sea Scrolls more fully (for example adding a paragraph to 1 Samuel 10 from 4QSama). An updated edition (NRSVue) appeared in 2021. It has Protestant, Catholic and Orthodox editions with differing sets of deuterocanonical books.
579: A team of scholars turned Kenneth Taylor's popular paraphrase, *The Living Bible* (1971), into a fresh meaning-based translation from Hebrew and Greek.
580: Aimed at clarity for modern readers, it was revised in 2004 and later. It is often used for public reading and for new readers.
583: The ESV revised the 1971 RSV toward a more literal, 'essentially literal' style and conservative evangelical choices, and quickly became widely used in Reformed and evangelical churches.
584: Changes from the RSV included 'virgin' in Isaiah 7:14 and other Christological readings of Old Testament passages. Revisions followed in 2007, 2011 and 2016 (which the publisher first called permanent, then reversed).
586: The NET Bible (first edition 2005, with about 60,000 translators' notes, free online) and the Holman Christian Standard Bible (2004, revised as the CSB in 2017) joined the crowded field of English translations.
587: The NET's notes openly show translation and text-critical choices, making it a teaching tool. The CSB aims for 'optimal equivalence', between formal and dynamic. The large number of English versions raises its own debate: some see helpful choice, others confusion and marketing.
590: NA28 (2012) and UBS5 (2014) updated the standard Greek text, incorporating the CBGM results for James to Jude.
591: Outside the Catholic Letters the main text was unchanged from NA27. The edition's apparatus lets readers see which manuscripts support each reading, a resource now also freely online.
592: The CBGM changes how editors choose readings
593: Münster, Germany (Institute for New Testament Textual Research)
